title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (N = 240 paired intents) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Tasks were drawn as 60% in‑distribution, 20% distribution‑shift, and 20% adversarial‑prompt, and the trial used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across paired arms). The guarded arm could invoke up to one validator‑triggered repair. All 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both arms: baseline_success_rate = 240/240 = 1.0, guarded_success_rate = 240/240 = 1.0; paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation shows no repair was invoked because every shared initial generation passed the deterministic validator. We report the preregistered design, execution accounting (shared initial generations = 240, model calls used = 240), analysis parameters (bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729), interpret the null result under shared_initial_candidate semantics, and give concrete design recommendations for future emulation‑grounded NetOps evaluations.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into concrete device configuration and to automate NetOps workflows. Execution‑grounded evaluations that place LLM agents into emulated networks show multi‑step planning and workflow failures that static text metrics miss [1]. A recurring mitigation architecture is generate–validate–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration, apply a deterministic validator, and invoke repair when the validator signals a violation [2,3]. We preregistered and ran a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment to measure whether adding a deterministic verifier (with up to one validator‑triggered repair) reduces unsafe configuration applications from a single LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline when the same initial LLM candidate is shared across paired arms. Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered paired confirmatory run (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) executed on an emulation benchmark; (2) archival of execution, per‑call traces, and analysis artifacts; and (3) a failure‑analytic interpretation of a null paired outcome together with concrete experiment‑design recommendations.
sections.related_work: Emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks and closed‑loop agent evaluations have been developed to reveal planning and execution faults in LLM agents [1]. Prior literature on automated configuration and program repair documents generate‑and‑validate patterns and reports practical gains under constrained settings, while noting semantic gaps that deterministic validators can miss [2,4]. Surveys and recent position work advocate tool augmentation (ReAct/agentic tool use), verifier gating, and uncertainty calibration to improve safety and operator trust, but highlight the need for tighter empirical evaluation of verifier impact under distribution shift and adversarial prompts [3,5]. Our study operationalizes a preregistered paired test of the GVR pattern in an emulation‑grounded setting and focuses on the specific operationally meaningful estimand specified below.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study preregistration (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) defined the primary estimand as the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate). Design and sampling: N = 240 distinct tasks executed as paired episodes (baseline LLM‑only vs guarded GVR). Task composition: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial 20% (48). Generation semantics and adapter contract: per the preregistered adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused for both arms; only a validator‑triggered repair (at most one permitted per task in the guarded arm) could create a paired divergence. Model and runtime settings: the declared_model_version was "gpt-5-mini"; the archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset) which does not imply deterministic sampling from the hosted provider—sampling nondeterminism remains possible and all model‑call metadata were recorded. Verifier and repair: the guarded arm used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and allowed up to one repair invocation per task. Budget and stopping: planned_episode_count = 480 (240 pairs × shared_initial semantics); maximum_model_calls = 480; the run followed the preregistered retry policy for infra failures. Scoring and analysis: episodes were deterministically executed in the emulator and scored safe (0) or unsafe (1) by the deterministic validator and simulator. Primary analysis used the registered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor with 10,000 bootstrap resamples (seed = 1729) for paired percentile CIs and an exact McNemar two‑sided test. Missingness/exclusion rules: preregistration excluded pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (verifier PASS with simulator unsafe outcome) from the primary analysis and specified sensitivity treatments; exclusions are reported when present.
sections.results: Execution accounting and reconciliation: the registered adapter completed the planned run: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240; hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 (one shared initial generation per task) and model_calls_used = 240 (provider call audit confirmed stage_counts {shared_initial_generation: 240}). Primary binary outcomes: baseline_success_count = 240/240 (success rate 1.0), guarded_success_count = 240/240 (success rate 1.0). Paired contingency: n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Inference: paired difference = 0.00; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Repair and call activity: no validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode (repair_attempts = 0); the guarded pipeline therefore produced identical final configurations to baseline for every pair because the single shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation for all tasks. Missingness and flags: analysis/missingness_summary.csv and analysis/contamination_summary.csv show zero infra failures and zero flagged 'possible false‑safe' items; consequently no preregistered exclusions affected the primary analysis.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and inferential scope: the preregistered primary hypothesis (H1: GVR reduces unsafe‑apply rate relative to LLM‑only) is not supported by these data; crucially, under shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm can only differ from baseline when the shared initial candidate fails validation or when a repair is applied. Because every shared initial candidate passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the guarded arm had no opportunity to alter any paired outcome and the paired contrast was degenerate (no discordant pairs). Statistically, n10 = n01 = 0 yields a degenerate McNemar test and a zero‑width bootstrap CI, which reflect execution facts rather than estimator failure. Design implications and recommendations: (1) To measure verifier benefit in a paired framework, relax shared_initial_candidate semantics (allow independent initial generation per arm) or permit a larger repair budget so generator variability can produce validator failures in at least one arm. (2) Increase adversary adaptivity and strength (beyond a single preregistered attacker seed) when testing guard efficacy against prompt injection. (3) Broaden verifier semantic coverage and instrument verifier false‑safe rates by routine cross‑checks against independent simulator outcomes. (4) Report repair counts, model‑call budgets, and latency to evaluate operational cost trade‑offs. Threats to validity: internal validity is limited by the shared_initial_candidate design and single‑model execution; construct validity is limited by the finite deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule set; external validity is limited by the emulation‑corpus scope and single‑model testing; conclusion validity is constrained because the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 made the preregistered primary contrast untestable in this run. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived to permit reanalysis under alternative generation semantics.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Every paired episode was safe under both LLM‑only and guarded arms, producing a paired difference of 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation confirms that no validator‑triggered repairs occurred because the single shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator for all tasks. The null result is informative: under shared_initial_candidate semantics a deterministic verifier can only affect paired outcomes when initial candidates fail validation or when the design permits generator variability between arms. We provide the preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call traces, and analysis artifacts to support follow‑up experiments that vary generation semantics, adversary strength, and verifier coverage.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: The experiment used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Runtime sampling: archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset); unset temperature does not imply deterministic sampling by the provider and sampling nondeterminism remains possible; all model‑call metadata were archived. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock; a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the lock; no manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred post‑lock. Preregistered generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); only validator‑triggered repairs could create paired divergences. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240. Immutable master prompt: the initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Reproducibility pointer: archived execution manifest and per‑call traces, task manifests, and analysis artifacts are available in the execution bundle (see execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/). This Disclosure provides the mandatory master‑prompt locator and concise autonomy summary; detailed per‑call traces and artifact hashes are archived in the manifest.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidates failing validation.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed attacker protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
